title: Should Dietary Planning Start from Energy? An Essential Amino Acid–First Framework
content: Amino acids serve functions beyond protein synthesis. Genetic information is expressed largely through proteins assembled from them; they constitute structural proteins, enzymes and immune proteins, serve as precursors of neurotransmitters and act as signalling molecules. Nine of them, the essential amino acids (EAAs), cannot be synthesised by the human body and have no dedicated store, so the diet must supply them every day. Nevertheless, dietary planning starts from an energy target, partitioned among carbohydrate, fat and protein, and assumes that EAA requirements are met within the protein allowance. We argue that dietary planning should start from the EAAs. An energy-first plan is easily met with energy-dense foods that often lack other essential nutrients, and can leave one or more EAAs below requirement. Such diets may meet the EAA requirements only when much more food, and therefore energy, is eaten. Under energy restriction, as during weight loss, and in older adults or those eating only plant foods, the same sequence can leave the limiting EAA short. Starting from the EAAs removes this dependence. Meeting all nine from a single food with a high EAA content takes 10–53% of daily energy (2,000 kcal) in our examples; the remaining energy can be adjusted to individual needs and goals. This sequence also fits physiology: energy requirements fluctuate from day to day and are buffered by glycogen and adipose tissue, whereas EAA requirements scale with body weight. A plan should be anchored to the more stable target, with the more variable one adjusted to it. The framework has four steps: Select, Combine, Complete and Adjust. It concerns the sequence in which a diet is planned, not the order in which foods are eaten; it is neither a high-protein nor a supplement-based diet and uses ordinary foods within any dietary pattern.
